To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
seedling survival and growth in high elevation forests are limited by water availability and that warming reduces survival via a reduction in growth and root development.
seedling establishment is inhibited by warming at the cold edge (tree line) of forests, and this is likely because of a lack of moisture stress tolerance in newly germinated seedings.

(1) tree seedlings have poor turgor loss and water use efficiency, which are correlated with growth; (2) growth is correlated with soil moisture status, particularly for small seeded species; and (3) seedlings of all three species had lower growth, allocation and survival under warming, particularly in drier conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how climate change may affect tree seedlings at the upper limit of forest in the Rocky Mountains.
the role of water availability and water use efficiency in limiting the establishment and growth of tree species at the upper limit of their elevational ranges.
the effects of climate change on forest tree regeneration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

warming can reduce seedling establishment across elevations via moisture limitation, but that species differ in the degree of this limitation, and that these species differences may be explained by their growth and drought tolerance attributes.
seedlings at the cold edge are more vulnerable to warming than those at the warm edge, but that the effects of warming vary with moisture status.

the effects of warming on growth and survival of seedlings are complex and depend on species and on interactions among temperature, water availability and soil moisture status, which vary across elevational gradients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
warming effects on tree regeneration are complex and depend on the species and the environment.
the growth strategies and drought tolerance of tree seedlings are important factors in determining their response to warming and water deficit.
warming reduces tree seedling establishment in high elevation forests via moisture stress.
The main takeaway from our work is that
seedling responses to warming vary with species and moisture availability and that seedlings are likely to be most susceptible to warming where soils are driest.

the effects of warming on the establishment of tree species in alpine environments may not be limited to the upper elevation limit of forests but could extend across the full gradient from subalpineto alpine.
the effects of warming on forest trees may be more complicated than predicted from the simple assumption of moisture limitation at lower elevations and temperature limitation at upper elevations.
